Who collects the tax

Your municipality decides. Some communities take the first installment themselves, and others have contracted with the Waukesha County Treasurer to take it. The county office is Room AC148 in the Administration Building, 515 W. Moreland Blvd., Waukesha, WI 53188. Call 262-548-7029, weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

Second installments are paid to the county treasurer everywhere, along with delinquent payments. You can pay by mail, online, or in the blue and white drive-up drop box on the east side of the Administration Building. A deposit made by 7:30 a.m. is dated the previous day.

Due dates by community

Most municipalities in the county use January 31 and July 31. A few allow three payments. The county's tax due date chart has the full list; this sample shows the pattern.

A three-payment plan exists because of a local ordinance, which Wis. Stat. 74.12 permits. The statute requires at least half the tax by April 30 and the rest by July 31. Miss any installment and the whole unpaid balance goes delinquent, so read your own bill instead of assuming the standard schedule.

Which communities pay the county first?

Under agreements with the county, a group of municipalities send first-installment checks to the Waukesha County Treasurer. The group includes the Town of Brookfield, City of Delafield, Town of Delafield, and the villages of Dousman, Elm Grove, Lannon, Lisbon, Menomonee Falls, Merton, Nashotah, North Prairie, Oconomowoc Lake, Pewaukee, Wales and Waukesha.

Everywhere else, you pay the local treasurer first. The county gets no tax information from the City of Waukesha until the first of the next year, so ask that city's treasurer for amounts. For most other communities, the county's online tax lookup carries current data through December.

Late taxes and the lien process

Late tax grows 1.5 percent a month from February 1. That is 1 percent interest plus a 0.5 percent penalty, both figured on the unpaid balance on the first business day of each month.

The county follows a fixed sequence:

  • February and August bring mailed statements of delinquent tax, interest and penalty.
  • On September 1 every property with unpaid current-year tax receives a tax certificate, a lien in the county's favor.
  • The certificate must be held two years before foreclosure may begin.
  • The in rem process under Wis. Stat. 75.521 adds in rem fees, and redeeming means paying all taxes, specials, interest, penalties and those fees.

The county also runs tax foreclosure auctions through WisconsinSurplus.com. If you are behind by more than a year, ask the treasurer for a written payoff before you list or sign a contract.

Mailing a payment and paying by card

A mailed payment is timely under Wis. Stat. 74.69(1) if it is postmarked before midnight on the deadline, carries postage and reaches the treasurer within five business days. A postage meter date is not a postmark.

Mail several days early, especially from a community mailbox, and ask a post office clerk to hand-cancel the envelope. Never mail cash. The office accepts cashier's checks, money orders, personal checks or cash in United States funds, and may ask for guaranteed funds. Online fees:

  • $1.50 for direct debit from a checking account
  • $3.95 for a debit card
  • 2.39 percent of the payment, $1.50 minimum, for a credit card

Mortgage escrow payments

An escrow check may be made out to the county treasurer, the local treasurer or the deeded owner. A check naming you jointly with a treasurer cannot be cashed by you, because it has to be applied to the tax.

If an escrow payment is more than the bill, the county notifies your local treasurer, who issues the refund. For an overpaid second installment, the county mails a check within thirty days. For a seller this means your lender may already have paid part of the year. Get a payment history from the servicer, then a current statement from the treasurer, so the figures at closing agree.

How do I challenge an assessment?

Your municipal assessor produced the value on the bill, and you object through your municipality's board of review. Wis. Stat. 70.47 has that board sitting for 45 days from the fourth Monday of April. Give notice at least 48 hours before the first meeting, and file a written objection during its first two hours.

The Department of Revenue sets an average assessment ratio for each municipality, comparing assessed value with equalized value. Divide your assessed value by that ratio and you get an estimate of fair market value, though taxes are not calculated from that figure. That explains why an assessed value can sit below market value.

Two credits lower the final bill. The lottery and gaming credit under Wis. Stat. 79.10 applies to qualifying homeowners, and the school levy tax credit is state-funded.

Selling a Waukesha County house

Waukesha County lies west of Milwaukee, and its suburbs grew after Interstate 94 was built. In 2020 it had 406,978 residents and 172,177 housing units, 4.4 percent of them vacant, and 75.2 percent of occupied homes are owner-occupied. Lake Country in the northwest includes Pewaukee, Delafield, Hartland, Merton, Nashotah, Chenequa, Oconomowoc, Summit and Lac La Belle. The county seat is Waukesha.

Your tax parcel number starts with two to four letters that identify the municipality, followed by six to ten digits. Keep it close when you call the treasurer for a payoff or a statement. Know too which office took your first installment, since that depends on where the parcel sits.

Paying off taxes at closing

Sellers with a balance should line up three things before the closing date: the servicer's payment history if a lender holds escrow, a current statement from the treasurer, and a written payoff if any tax is delinquent. Because interest is figured on the first business day of each month, ask for a payoff that matches the month you close. Hand all three to the closing agent. A cash buyer skips the lender's escrow reconciliation, but the title company still wants the treasurer's statement before it releases funds.

Frequently asked questions

When are Waukesha County property taxes due?

Most municipalities use January 31 and July 31. The City of Waukesha, City of New Berlin and Village of Sussex use January 31, March 31 and May 31 and collect those payments themselves.

How much interest is charged on delinquent taxes?

1.5 percent per month on the unpaid balance, counted back to February 1. That is made up of 1 percent interest and a 0.5 percent penalty.

Where do I mail my tax payment?

To Waukesha County Treasurer, 515 W. Moreland Blvd., Room AC148, Waukesha, WI 53188 when the county is collecting. If your municipality collects its own first installment, mail it to that treasurer.

What is a tax certificate?

A lien the county issues each September 1 on properties with unpaid current-year taxes. It must be held two years before foreclosure can begin, and paying the full delinquency for that tax year voids it.

Can I pay by card?

Yes, online. Direct debit costs $1.50, a debit card $3.95 and a credit card 2.39 percent with a $1.50 minimum. In person, the office accepts cashier's checks, money orders, personal checks and cash.

Who collects property tax in Brown County, WI?

Who you pay turns on your municipality and the month. The Brown County Treasurer takes first-installment payments for just 12 municipalities, and 13 others handle their own. After the first installment, unpaid and second-half taxes go to the county treasurer.

Find the Treasurer at 305 E. Walnut Street, Room 160, in Green Bay (zip 54301), or write to the post office box, number 23600, zip 54305. The phone line is 920-448-4074. The counter is open from half past seven in the morning until five in the afternoon Monday through Thursday, and until half past eleven on Friday morning. The office keeps property tax records, collects taxes, and handles delinquent taxes and foreclosures.

Section 74.11(6) directs money paid by January 31 to the taxation district treasurer, with everything later going to the county. Your bill names the payee, so read it before mailing.

Municipalities that collect their own taxes

Thirteen places collect their own first-installment taxes for the winter installment. A parcel in one of them pays the local city, village or town, not the county treasurer.

  • Cities: Green Bay (green bills) and De Pere (white bills).
  • Villages: Ashwaubenon, Bellevue, Denmark, Hobart, Howard, Pulaski and Suamico.
  • Towns: Holland, Ledgeview, Morrison and Rockland.

The county treasurer collects the winter installment for everyone else, and those are the Brown bills:

  • Towns: Eaton, Glenmore, Green Bay, Humboldt, Lawrence, New Denmark, Pittsfield, Scott and Wrightstown.
  • Villages: Allouez, Greenleaf and Wrightstown.

Names repeat here. Wrightstown is both a town and a village, and Green Bay is both a city and a town. Match the full name on your bill before you pay.

When are Brown County property taxes due?

Expect the bill near December 10. Under s. 74.11(2) you can pay in two installments, January 31 and July 31, or send the full amount by January 31. Municipalities have until the third Monday in December to mail, and this year that Monday is December 21 (s. 74.09(5)).

Weekends shift the practical deadlines. January 31, 2027 is a Sunday and July 31, 2027 is a Saturday. Five working days of grace follow the due date, and a due date on a weekend means the grace period ends at close of business on the first Friday of the following month.

StepDate

Pay half, or pay the full amountJanuary 31, 2027
Grace period ends, first installmentFriday, February 5, 2027
Second installment dueJuly 31, 2027
Grace period ends, second installmentFriday, August 6, 2027

Small bills, under $100, are paid whole by January 31. Some municipalities adopt an ordinance for three or more installments, with half in by April 30 and the rest by July 31 (s. 74.12), so your own bill sets your schedule.

What happens when a Brown County tax payment is late?

Skip the first installment and the whole unpaid balance turns delinquent on February 1. Skip the second and the unpaid balance turns delinquent on August 1. Once delinquent, real property tax is paid to the county treasurer, and interest and penalties are counted from the previous February 1 (s. 74.11(11)).

A bill that never showed up changes nothing, because s. 74.09(6) says a missing bill does not affect the tax or its collection. If mid-December passes with no bill, phone the treasurer or your municipal clerk. Selling a parcel that is already delinquent? Expect a payoff quote that includes interest.

How is a Brown County assessment set, and how do you appeal it?

A local assessor sets your value from the property's market value as of January 1. If you disagree, the formal appeal begins at your municipality's Board of Review under s. 70.47. The Department of Revenue's Guide for Property Owners, posted on the Brown County Treasurer's forms page, walks through each step.

  • Go to the assessor's open book first. After that, any change to the roll takes the Board of Review or a court.
  • Board of Review sessions happen once a year in a 45-day span starting the fourth Monday of April.
  • Notify the board clerk of your plan to object, by voice or on paper, no later than 48 hours before the first session.
  • Turn in a signed written objection on form PA-115A during the first two hours of the session, unless the board excuses the timing for good cause.
  • Bring evidence, because the board presumes the assessor's value is right until shown otherwise.

If the board rules against you, the circuit court can review the written record by certiorari if you ask within 90 days of the notice. You may also bring an excessive assessment claim under s. 74.37. It goes to the municipality by January 31 of the year the tax is payable, and it is off the table once you have taken the board's decision to court.

Help with a Brown County tax bill

State programs can reduce or defer a bill, and the Brown County Treasurer handles one of them directly.

  • Lottery and gaming credit: the Brown County Treasurer receives only forms LC-100 and LC-400.
  • Homestead credit: a credit based on income, open to owners and renters, handled by the Department of Revenue at 608-266-8641.
  • Deferral loan for elderly homeowners: administered by WHEDA at 800-755-7835. The loan becomes a lien, and repayment is due at sale or when you move out.
  • First dollar credit: appears on the bill as a cut in the tax due.

If a deferral loan is in place and you plan to sell, tell your title company early, since the loan is repaid when ownership transfers.

Property tax steps at a Brown County closing

Request a tax figure from the title company or closing agent before signing, and divide the current-year bill as the purchase contract says. Winter bills go out in December, so a fall closing lands close to bill season.

  • Find the parcel number and the correct payee on the latest bill.
  • Find out from the treasurer if an earlier year carries a delinquent balance.
  • Confirm whether your municipality pays in two installments or more.
  • Keep the receipt for any installment already paid and hand it to the closer.

The deed itself is recorded at the register of deeds. On a taxable sale the state's transfer fee, $3 per $1,000 of value, falls on the seller.

Selling with a cash buyer

Brown County sellers who need speed sometimes choose a cash buyer. Without a lender there is no underwriting queue, so the closing date hinges mostly on title work and how fast you produce paperwork. Tax tasks are unchanged. Confirm the payee, find out where each installment stands and get a payoff for any delinquent year. Call the local treasurer if your municipality takes its own first installment, and the county after that. Keeping both phone numbers handy stops a quick closing from stalling over a tax question.

Frequently asked questions

When are Brown County property taxes due?

Two installments: January 31 and July 31, or the entire bill by January 31. Bills go out around December 10. The statute adds five working days of grace, and a weekend due date pushes the cutoff to the first Friday of the next month.

Who gets my Brown County payment?

That varies by municipality. Thirteen cities, villages and towns collect their own first installment, including Green Bay and De Pere. The county treasurer collects for the other 12, such as Allouez and the Town of Scott. Anything later goes to the county treasurer.

Who sets my property tax assessment in Brown County?

A local assessor in your municipality, using market value as of January 1. To contest it, tell the Board of Review clerk 48 hours ahead of the first session, then file a written objection in that session's opening two hours.

What if I miss the Brown County January deadline?

When the payment has not arrived within five working days of the due date, the entire unpaid balance becomes delinquent as of February 1. The county treasurer then collects them, with interest and penalties dating from February 1.

Can I get help paying a Brown County property tax bill?

Possibly. The state offers an income-based homestead credit at 608-266-8641, a deferral loan for elderly homeowners through WHEDA at 800-755-7835, the lottery and gaming credit, and the first dollar credit. The county treasurer receives lottery and gaming forms LC-100 and LC-400.

Who bills and who collects

Your municipality mails the Racine County bill and takes the first payment, and the county treasurer picks up from there. Notices go out in December. Outside the City of Racine you may split the bill into two installments, January 31 and July 31, with the first one paid locally.

You will find the county treasurer on the courthouse's 1st floor, north end, at 730 Wisconsin Avenue, open weekdays from 8:00 am until 4:30 pm. The phone is (262) 636-3239 and the email is rctreasurer@racinecounty.gov. A county directory lists the clerk or treasurer for each of the Towns of Burlington, Dover, Norway and Waterford, the Villages of Caledonia, Elmwood Park, Mount Pleasant, North Bay, Raymond, Rochester, Sturtevant, Union Grove, Waterford, Wind Point and Yorkville, and the Cities of Burlington and Racine.

Racine County for a home seller

Racine County is a Lake Michigan county of about 198,919 people (2025 estimate), and 67.7 percent of occupied homes are owned by the people living in them. Lakeshore city streets, suburban villages and farm towns all sit inside one border. That means neighbors a few miles apart may pay on different schedules and answer to different assessors. Confirm your municipality first, then quote dates to a buyer.

Offices a seller should contact

A sale touches the assessor, a treasurer, the Register of Deeds and the Board of Review clerk. County-level contacts are below.

Ways to pay

The county treasurer accepts payment four ways: at the window, in the courthouse drop box, by mail, or online. Cash, checks and money orders work at the window. Leave only checks in the drop box on the east side facing Wisconsin Avenue, because cash is not accepted there. Mail checks to Racine County Treasurer, 730 Wisconsin Ave, Racine, WI 53403-1274.

  • Card or e-check: dial (800) 272-9829 or pay at OfficialPayments.com with jurisdiction code 5835. Third-party fees apply.
  • Record search: the Ascent Land Records site displays your tax record, and paying there takes the 15-digit parcel ID or tax key number.
  • Alerts: text and email notices can be set up for a parcel.

Brochures on paying real estate taxes, taxpayer help and tax foreclosure sit on the treasurer's pages, along with a glossary and a short guide to pulling your payment history.

Late or short installments

Pay late or pay too little and the whole remaining balance comes due immediately. Charges begin February 1: 1 percent interest and a 0.5 percent penalty each month, or 1.5 percent combined (Wis. Stat. s. 74.47). The treasurer cannot waive them.

There is a small grace period. Section 74.11(7) treats the first installment as delinquent only after five working days past January 31 go by unpaid. The county still counts interest from February 1 once you miss, so aim for January 31 itself.

Owners already behind are urged to set up regular payments, and the office takes monthly payments on delinquent bills. Get a payoff figure before you set a closing date.

Tax foreclosure sales

Racine County takes properties through tax foreclosure and then sells them at public sales run by the County Treasurer. There are three kinds: sealed bid, subsequent sealed bid and over-the-counter. You can join a buyers' email list for sale notices, and the Sheriff's Sale site covers sheriff's sales separately.

A Tax Foreclosure FAQ brochure is available from the treasurer. If several years are unpaid and you want to sell, closing before foreclosure begins gives you the most room. Ask which years are open and what clears them.

How to challenge your assessment

A disagreement over value is settled at your municipality's Board of Review, not at the treasurer's counter. Every town, village and city has its own board, and its clerk must post notice 15 days ahead of the first session (30 days in a revaluation year). Call the clerk each spring for dates.

  • Give the clerk written or oral notice 48 hours before the first meeting, or show good cause in the meeting's first two hours.
  • Hand in a written objection during those same two hours.
  • Challenge the combined land and building value, since s. 70.47(7)(a) rules out objecting to only one part.
  • Plan to be sworn in. Owners and their witnesses are heard first.

Tax credits that lower a bill

Two credits are worth checking. A lottery and gaming credit cuts the bill on a qualifying home, managed through the state revenue department's online portal, where late claims are due by October 1.

The homestead credit works differently: it is filed with your Wisconsin income tax return and helps lower-income households with property tax or rent. A fact sheet linked from the county explains eligibility, and a veteran's credit page is linked too.

Recording a deed at the Register of Deeds

Documents reach the Register of Deeds, also at 730 Wisconsin Avenue, by drop-off, mail or e-filing. Sellers who skip e-filing are told to go through a title company or an e-recording service provider. Self-serve search computers run 8:30 am to 4:00 pm and staff cannot run searches for you.

Costs are fixed by statute: $30 to record (s. 59.43(2)(ag)), plus a transfer fee of 30 cents per $100 of value (s. 77.22). Passing property by will or survivorship carries no fee, and some family transfers for token consideration are exempt as well.

Selling with taxes owed

Take it in this order.

  1. Look up the parcel and list the unpaid years.
  2. Ask whichever treasurer holds your installments for a full payoff, interest included.
  3. Pass the number to the title company so it is paid from your proceeds.
  4. File the transfer return and record the deed.

The calendar depends on location. City of Racine homes have four installments, while Mount Pleasant and Caledonia homes have two. From August 1 onward everything, city parcels included, is paid to the county.

A cash buyer or a financed buyer will both need the payoff, deed and transfer return. Compare every figure with the county tax record before you say yes to an offer.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I pay Racine County property taxes?

First installments go to your local municipality. Second installments and back taxes go to the county treasurer at 730 Wisconsin Avenue. The City of Racine takes its own four installments through July 31.

What is the Racine County treasurer's phone number?

It is (262) 636-3239. Walk-in hours at the courthouse, 730 Wisconsin Avenue, are weekdays 8:00 am to 4:30 pm.

What interest do late taxes carry in Racine County?

Each month adds 1 percent interest and a 0.5 percent penalty, 1.5 percent in all. The county has no authority to forgive it.

Can I pay Racine County taxes by card?

Yes. Call (800) 272-9829 or use OfficialPayments.com with jurisdiction code 5835. Third-party fees apply, and the drop box does not accept cash.

What does it cost to record a deed in Racine County?

The recording charge is $30, and the transfer fee is 30 cents per $100 of value unless an exemption applies. The Register of Deeds can confirm at (262) 636-3208.

Dane County at a glance

Dane County is large, urban and divided among many taxing bodies, and Madison collects its own current-year tax. The 2020 count was 561,504 residents, second in Wisconsin after Milwaukee County, with nearly 10% of the state's people. Madison is both county seat and state capital.

Housing leans toward renting more than most of the state. In 2020 there were 248,795 housing units and 238,417 households, with 56.3% of occupied units owner-occupied and 43.7% rented. The homeowner vacancy rate was 0.8% and the rental vacancy rate 3.9%.

  • Villages: Belleville, Black Earth, Blue Mounds, Brooklyn, Cambridge, Cottage Grove, Cross Plains, Dane, Deerfield, DeForest, Maple Bluff, Marshall, Mazomanie, McFarland, Mount Horeb, Oregon, Rockdale, Shorewood Hills, Waunakee and Windsor.

Due dates

The first payment is due January 31 and the final one July 31. Municipalities mail bills on the third Monday of December, the same day Access Dane is updated with the new tax data.

The yearly cycle runs like this. Assessors set values as of January 1, taxing districts adopt budgets in the fall, and in December each assessment is multiplied by the mill rate to get total tax. The lottery credit and first dollar credit come off to give net property tax, and special assessments and special charges are added to produce the bill.

Owners pay at different times: roughly 30% in full in December, 40% in full in January and 30% in installments. Madison works differently, with intermediate installments and the City Treasurer collecting through July 31. The Madison treasurer is at 210 Martin Luther King Jr Blvd, Room 107, phone (608) 266-4771.

Late payment penalty

A missed payment makes the entire bill due at once, and interest and penalty together of 1.5% of the unpaid principal are added back to February 1. The charge accrues at the start of each month until everything is paid.

Someone late on the final installment still owes the charge reaching back to February 1. A payment in August therefore carries seven months of it, and each later month adds another 1.5%.

The postmark decides timeliness, and the Postal Service does not postmark mail the day it is dropped off. Near a deadline you have these options:

  • Pay by e-Check or credit card on the Treasurer's website.
  • Mail a check to Dane County Treasurer, PO Box 1299, Madison, WI 53701-1299, early enough to be postmarked on time.
  • If you pay through your bank, schedule it 7 to 10 business days ahead.

Delinquent tax needs its own check made out to Dane County. A payment is not final until it clears the bank, and a returned payment cancels the bills it covered.

How to appeal your assessment

Begin with a conversation with your municipal assessor. If you still disagree, take it to the municipal Board of Review. Once that board has acted, it is normally too late to contest the value for that year.

The Notice of Assessment generally shows up in March or later. During the Open Book period you can go over the numbers with the assessor. Formal appeals are heard by the Board of Review in a quasi-judicial setting, under rules in Wisconsin Statute 70.47:

  • The board meets in the 45 days after the fourth Monday of April.
  • Give notice at least 48 hours ahead, then file a written objection in the first two hours of the opening meeting, unless the board waives the rule.
  • An owner who turned down the assessor's reasonable certified-mail request to view the exterior cannot appear.
  • For income-method properties, send the assessor the income and expense data requested no later than 7 days before the first meeting.
  • If the board waives its hearing, you have 60 days from the notice of waiver to start an excessive assessment action under Statute 74.37(3)(d).

The treasurer's page links the Department of Revenue Guide for Property Owners and the Board of Review Member Guide. Every city, village and town runs its own board, so the local clerk gives you the date.

Parcels that went to tax deed

A former owner can buy the property back before the public auction, and the county sells what it took as is. Dane County does not sell tax deeds or tax liens. It sells properties it acquired through the tax deed process under Wisconsin Statute 75.35.

Auctions usually take place in October or November, and sometimes again in April or May, by sealed bid. Bids are due on a Tuesday at 1:00 pm and opened the next day at 10:00 am in the Treasurer's office. Each bid needs a form and a 10% earnest deposit, payment is cash or cashier's check only, and the buyer has ten days after the award notice to close.

Former owners can repurchase up to two weeks before the bid due date. If the parcel sells at auction, the county returns any net proceeds to the former owner. Occupants may still be living in a parcel at the time of a fall auction, and the county notes occupant status for each parcel. The Treasurer's office asks people not to phone for sale details, so read the Tax Deed Auction page first.

Selling with taxes owed

Confirm the balance with the correct treasurer, pay it at closing, and record the deed with the transfer return. Who you call depends on where the house is, since a Madison parcel and one in Sun Prairie or Verona follow different routes.

  • Locate the parcel number on the tax bill, or search Access Dane by address.
  • For Madison parcels, call the City of Madison Treasurer. For others, ask the local municipal treasurer about tax due through January 31, and the Dane County Treasurer about the July 31 installment and any delinquent tax.
  • Record the deed at the Register of Deeds, phone (608) 266-4141, with the electronic Wisconsin Real Estate Transfer Return. The fee is 30 cents per $100 of value under Statute 77.22(1), paid by the grantor.
  • After closing, update the mailing address in writing with Dane County Planning and Development, Property Listing, Room 116, or by email to property.listing@danecounty.gov.

If an owner has died, the name comes off the record by a recorded Termination of Decedent's Interest for joint tenancy or survivorship marital property, or a Final Judgment for tenants in common. A transfer by will, descent or survivorship is exempt from the transfer fee under Statute 77.25(11). A cash buyer skips the lender, but the tax payoff still happens at closing.

Frequently asked questions

When are Dane County property taxes due?

January 31 is the first due date and July 31 the final one. January payments go to your municipality and July payments to the Dane County Treasurer, except City of Madison properties, which the City Treasurer collects through July 31.

What penalty applies to late Dane County property tax?

Interest and penalty combined come to 1.5% of unpaid principal per month, added back to February 1. A missed installment makes the full amount due, and a payment in August carries seven months of the charge.

Where do I pay Dane County property tax in person?

At the Dane County Treasurer's office in the City-County Building, Room 114, 210 Martin Luther King Jr Blvd, Madison. It is open 8:00 to 4:00 Monday through Friday, holidays excluded, and has a drop box.

Can I appeal my Dane County assessment after the Board of Review?

Usually not for that year. After the Board of Review it would normally be too late. Talk to your assessor during the Open Book period and file with the board on time.

How do I change the billing address on a Dane County parcel?

Contact the municipal clerk or treasurer, or write to Dane County Planning and Development, Property Listing, Room 116, 210 Martin Luther King Jr Blvd, Madison, WI 53703. Email to property.listing@danecounty.gov also works.

Who handles property tax in Rock County?

Three offices touch a Rock County bill. Your municipal assessor sets the value, the Real Property Description office keeps parcel records, and the Rock County Treasurer collects nearly all of the money. The Treasurer is in the Courthouse at 51 South Main Street, Janesville, WI 53545, open Monday to Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The phone number is 608-757-5670.

Real Property Description serves every municipality except the City of Beloit and the City of Janesville. That split matters when you move or sell: address changes for Beloit and Janesville go to the Treasurer, and changes for the other 27 municipalities go to Real Property.

The December tax notice tells you where and when to pay. If none has arrived by December 27, call the Treasurer or your local treasurer. The tax is owed whether or not the bill reaches you.

Rock County housing in brief

Rock County stretches over 726 square miles on the Illinois border, and Janesville is both the seat and the biggest city. Roughly 71% of homes are lived in by their owners. An estimated 166,472 people lived here in mid-2025, in 72,312 housing units. Owner-occupied homes have a median value of $231,600, and gross rent has a median of $1,037. Those numbers give a rough sense of where a typical house will price, though your own assessor's figure and local comparable sales matter more.

When taxes are due

Two dates cover most owners, January 31 and July 31, and Beloit adds two more. A bill above $100 may be split, half by January 31 and half by July 31, or paid whole in January. At $100 or under, the full amount is due January 31 (s. 74.11(7) or 74.12). Personal property tax is also due whole on January 31.

  • Everywhere but Beloit: first or full payment January 31, then the second installment July 31, which only the County Treasurer takes.
  • Beloit: four installments, each paid to the County Treasurer.

Through December and January, four towns collect the first payment themselves. Once January 31 passes, the County Treasurer collects for all municipalities, and mailing a check to a local treasurer after that is discouraged.

Late payments and how to pay

Skip one installment and you lose the installment option, with the full unpaid amount turning delinquent. From February 1 the rate is 1.5% monthly, so 18% yearly, and a partial month is billed as a whole one.

Only United States Postal Service postmarks count with the Treasurer, not metered ones. A check mailed on the final day should be hand canceled at the post office counter. Make checks out to the Rock County Treasurer. Cash is taken at the counter only.

  • GovTech Services processes cards and e-checks, charging 2.29% on credit, $3.95 on debit and $1.00 per e-check.
  • To pay by phone, call 1-855-912-7625. Electronic payments can take 5 to 10 business days to arrive.
  • A first payment owed to a town treasurer cannot go through GovTech.
  • One Courthouse drop box sits before security, and another is beside the Treasurer's door on the second floor.

Homeowners with escrow still get the notice. Confirm the lender's payment date, and ask for its tax escrow option notice if you prefer a different one.

Challenging your assessment

Your assessor's valuation notice lists the first protest steps. Dates come from your own clerk, since each municipality schedules its own. The Department of Revenue's Guide for Property Owners and s. 70.47 lay out the statewide process.

  • Raise questions with the assessor at open book. After that, changes require a formal process.
  • The Board of Review sits during a 45-day period that starts the fourth Monday in April, no sooner than seven days after open book.
  • Tell the clerk 48 hours before the first meeting, then submit the signed form PA-115A during the first two hours. The notice can be waived for good cause.
  • You object to land and buildings as one total, and the board presumes the assessor's number is correct until shown otherwise.
  • After a ruling you can appeal to the Department of Revenue (s. 70.85) within 20 days of delivery for a $100 fee, or file in circuit court (s. 70.47(13)) within 90 days.
  • A claim of excessive assessment (s. 74.37) requires that you appeared before the Board of Review first, and it must reach the municipality by January 31 of the year the tax is due.

You can also attend the budget meetings of your school district, technical college, county and municipality, because those budgets set the levy.

Credits and relief

Relief here comes from state credits and one loan program, with no separate county exemption. Each agency handles its own applications.

  • Income tax credits through the Department of Revenue: Homestead, Farmland Tax Relief and School Property Tax.
  • Farmland Preservation Credit, from the state agriculture department (DATCP).
  • WHEDA property tax deferral loans for the elderly, 1-800-755-7835.
  • Credits printed on the bill itself: Lottery and Gaming, First Dollar, and School Levy Tax.

Eligibility and deadlines shift, so pick up the current form before counting on a credit in your payoff math.

Before closing on a Rock County house

Ask the Treasurer for what you owe now, with interest, in writing, and pass it to the title company so the closing statement agrees with county records. Owners who are behind keep accruing 1.5% each month until paid.

Names on bills follow deeds. County records reflect the latest recorded document, so a buyer shows up on later bills only once the Register of Deeds has recorded the deed. Walk-ins are welcome there, and the Courthouse lobby has a drop box.

Wisconsin also requires sellers of one to four unit homes to deliver a finished real estate condition report within 10 days of contract acceptance. Without it, the buyer may back out within two business days after the 10 days end (s. 709.02). One part of the form covers taxes, special assessments and permits, so gather those papers first.

Inheriting the house, having tenants or lacking repair money does not change this. Both the tax balance and the report go with the sale however it is structured.

Frequently asked questions

When is the first Rock County property tax payment due?

January 31 is the first deadline. A parcel over $100 can be paid half then and half by July 31, or whole in January. Beloit has four: January 31, March 31, May 31 and July 31.

Where do I send Rock County property tax?

Send it to the Rock County Treasurer, 51 South Main Street, Janesville. The exception is a parcel in the Town of Bradford, Janesville, Magnolia or Rock, whose first payment goes to the town. The county takes everything after January 31, and your bill names the right place.

How much interest does Rock County charge on late tax?

The charge is 1.5% a month starting February 1, and part of a month counts as a full one. A single missed installment puts the whole remaining balance in delinquency.

How do I protest my Rock County assessed value?

Start with the steps on the assessor's notice. If open book does not fix it, go to the Board of Review: give the clerk 48 hours' notice and file the objection form early in the first meeting. Dates come from your municipal clerk.

Can I sell a Rock County house before the property tax is paid?

Yes, once the unpaid amount is cleared with the Treasurer. A written balance given to the closing agent lets the payoff come out of your proceeds. Chapter 709 also requires the seller's condition report.

  • File the written objection inside the first two hours of that meeting.
  • Bring proof. The assessor's number is presumed right until you rebut it.

The board cannot be skipped. An excessive assessment claim under Wis. Stat. 74.37 goes to the municipal clerk by January 31 of the year the tax is payable, and you must have used the board process and paid on time. The municipality gets 90 days to answer. A denial opens a 90-day period, counted from the notice, to sue in circuit court.

State credits on the bill

Walworth County bills may show two state credits. One is the lottery and gaming credit, for owners who lived in the home as their primary residence on January 1 of the levy year. The other is the First Dollar Credit, which covers state taxable parcels carrying a real property improvement, in effect since the 2008 tax bill.

Details for both are with the Wisconsin Department of Revenue. When a credit you expect is missing, the county treasurer or your local treasurer can tell you how to apply.

Selling in Walworth County

The county lies against the Illinois line, and Elkhorn is the seat. It counted 106,478 residents and 53,146 housing units in 2020, with 20.3 percent of units vacant and 31.1 percent of occupied homes rented. Lake Geneva tourism feeds a busy second-home market.

Several municipalities straddle county lines. Burlington sits mostly in Racine County, Whitewater partly in Jefferson County, Genoa City partly in Kenosha County and Mukwonago mostly in Waukesha County. Check the county named on your tax bill before choosing which treasurer to phone.

Ahead of a cash closing, have the closing agent ask the treasurer for a current tax statement so any balance for the year is paid at the table. Also note which installments you have paid and to whom: the January payment went to the municipality, and the July payment goes to the county. Bring the bill stub and parcel number when you talk to either office, and ask the closing agent how the year's tax will be prorated between you and the buyer.

A short to-do list before listing

First, find the parcel number, tax key number and municipality printed on the bill. Next, learn whether the first payment is already in. Then phone the local treasurer, or the county treasurer after the January window, and ask for the balance and any interest. If the parcel is behind, add the payoff to your list of closing costs. Last, give the closing agent the figures in writing so the settlement statement matches what the treasurer will actually accept. These steps take an afternoon and prevent surprises on closing day.

Frequently asked questions

What are the two payment dates in Walworth County?

January 31 for the full tax or the first half, July 31 for the second half. A bill below $100 is due in full in January. The local municipality gets the first payment and the Walworth County Treasurer gets the second.

How do I reach the Walworth County Treasurer?

Room 103 of the Government Center, 100 W Walworth Street, Elkhorn, WI 53121; phone 262-741-4251. Send mail to P.O. Box 1001, Elkhorn, WI 53121. The counter opens 8 am to 4:30 pm on weekdays.

What does a late Walworth County payment cost?

Each month adds 1 percent interest and a 0.5 percent penalty, for 1.5 percent altogether. Counting begins February 1, and a part of a month is charged as a full month.

Can Walworth County take a house over unpaid tax?

Yes, after two or more years of delinquency, through the in rem procedure. Interested parties redeem by covering the amount owed and costs ahead of the redemption date in the published notice.

Who do I ask about a value I dispute?

Your local assessor, followed by the municipal board of review. Assessed values are not set or changed at the county treasurer's office.

Who collects the tax

In St. Croix County the treasurer's office does most of the work: it takes payments for 18 municipalities, accepts every second-half and late payment countywide, and keeps the tax rolls with assessed values. Visit the Government Center, 1101 Carmichael Road, Hudson, or phone 715-386-4645.

The same office prepares tax deed applications and manages credits. Valuation happens at the municipal level; your clerk can name your assessor. If the name or parcel description on your bill looks wrong, the Real Property Listing office (715-386-4680) is the place to ask.

One statement per parcel is printed each year and sent to whoever owned the property at that moment. A sale after printing triggers no second mailing, so a buyer closing in that gap should request a duplicate from the treasurer or the local clerk.

Due dates and penalties

You can pay everything by January 31 or split the bill: half by January 31 and half by July 31. Wisconsin taxes run a year behind. A bill issued in December 2026 covers 2026 and becomes payable starting January 31, 2027. Expect the envelope in mid-December.

The rules sit in Wis. Stat. 74.11. A bill under $100 has to be settled in one payment by January 31. If the first half has not reached the office within five working days of January 31, the entire remaining balance goes delinquent on February 1. January 31, 2027 falls on a Sunday, so that five-day window closes at the end of business on Friday, February 5. Still, plan around January 31 itself, because payments count as on time when they are received by the due date.

Once a balance is delinquent the charge is 1.5% per month starting February 1, with any part of a month rounded up to a full one. The statute behind it, Wis. Stat. 74.47, fixes interest at 1% monthly and lets the county board tack on a penalty of up to 0.5% monthly. Payment plans are not offered here. Paying in part is still smart, and the law accepts partial payments of $20 or more against delinquent taxes.

Where to send the first installment

Where your check goes in January depends on where the parcel sits. Some municipalities route the first payment to the county treasurer, while others keep it locally. Here is a sample of the split.

Some towns, including Baldwin, Cady, Cylon and Emerald, also take their own January payment. No matter the municipality, the county treasurer receives July payments and anything overdue. A parcel in a place not shown above? Call 715-386-4645.

Ways to pay a St. Croix County bill

  • Counter or drop box: bring the bill details with your payment. The box is at 1101 Carmichael Road.
  • Portal: look up the parcel by number, by address or by name, one search term at a time.

Mail a few days ahead of any deadline, because postal delays are your problem, not the county's. Need the bill sent somewhere else? The county has a change of address form.

How do you appeal a St. Croix County assessment?

Your first stop is the board of review run by your own town, village or city, not the county. Under Wis. Stat. 70.47 it convenes yearly during a 45-day stretch that begins the fourth Monday of April.

Before the meeting, the assessor must mail notice of a changed value: at least 15 days ahead normally, and 30 days ahead in a revaluation year. Missing the notice in your mailbox leaves the assessment standing. To object, work through this list:

  • Warn the board clerk, by voice or in writing, at least 48 hours before the opening meeting.
  • Hand the clerk a signed objection on the board's form during the first two hours of that meeting.
  • State, in writing, what you think the land is worth and what the improvements are worth, with the information behind your figures.
  • Testify under oath. Until you rebut it, the board assumes the assessor got the value right.

With a house on the land, the combined figure is what you contest, not the lot or building alone. Testifying is off the table if you refused the assessor's written request to view the exterior.

Lottery and gaming credit

For a home you live in, the biggest break is the state lottery and gaming credit. To get it you must be a Wisconsin resident who owns the dwelling and treats it as your primary residence on January 1. Nothing is automatic, so file for it. A credit that did not appear on your bill can still be claimed through the municipal treasurer by January 31, or late through the Department of Revenue by October 1.

Rentals, empty land and garages do not count. When the house sells, the credit stays on the parcel, so it is part of the tax proration between buyer and seller, and a buyer who moves in files a fresh application. The county treasurer can tell you if your parcel receives it.

If taxes go unpaid

Unpaid taxes can end in a tax deed taken by the county. Parcels it ends up owning are offered by sealed bid, with a 10% deposit, the balance due 30 days after the award, and a quit claim deed, as is.

You have choices long before that. Wis. Stat. 74.51 lets anyone clear delinquent taxes ahead of a tax certificate by paying what is due plus interest and any penalty. Under Wis. Stat. 74.53 the county may also take a former owner to court over taxes that went unpaid during that person's ownership, and co-owners share the liability.

Ask the treasurer for a payoff figure before listing. Give the number to your closing agent so it comes out of proceeds at closing and the buyer receives a clean parcel.

Selling a St. Croix County house

The county borders Minnesota, Hudson is its seat, and it belongs to the Minneapolis-St. Paul metro area. Population is 98,276 (2025 estimate), up 5.1% from April 2020. A typical owner-occupied home is valued at $377,700, and 78.3% of housing units are lived in by their owners.

Some errands pay off. Phone the treasurer for the balance, and confirm who took the January payment, since it may have gone to a local treasurer while the July one goes to the county. Keep your parcel number handy for every call. A cash buyer skips lender appraisal and financing delays, which helps when a payoff or deed problem is already eating the calendar.

Frequently asked questions

When is the second installment due in St. Croix County?

July 31, paid to the St. Croix County Treasurer. If it is not received within five working days after that date, the entire unpaid balance goes delinquent August 1 under Wis. Stat. 74.11(8).

How much interest is charged on late property tax?

The charge is 1.5% a month counting from February 1, and a partial month is billed as a full one. State law sets the base at 1% monthly, and a county board may add as much as 0.5% as a penalty.

Can I set up a payment plan with the treasurer?

No, the office runs no payment plans. You are urged to pay whatever you can, and partial payments of $20 or more are accepted on delinquent taxes.

Who handles a property tax appeal?

Your municipal board of review. Tell its clerk at least 48 hours before the first meeting, then file a written objection in the first two hours. The board meets within a 45-day period that starts the fourth Monday of April.

Do I get a new tax bill if I buy a house after bills are printed?

No. Ownership changes recorded after printing produce no new statement, and the bill goes to the owner on record. As a buyer, ask the treasurer for a copy.

Who collects property tax

Two offices share the work. The Milwaukee County Treasurer takes delinquent taxes for 2024 and earlier from every municipality but the City of Milwaukee, and the City Treasurer handles both current and late bills for parcels inside the city.

The Milwaukee County market

Milwaukee County is Wisconsin's most populous and most densely populated county. The 2020 census counted 939,489 residents, and the July 2025 estimate is 924,216, a decline of 1.6 percent. There are 429,425 housing units. Only 49.9 percent of households own, so about half rent. Expect the buyer's title company to search the parcel for back taxes, so see what the Treasurer's records show before listing.

Due dates and penalties

Paying in two pieces? The state's 2026 Guide for Property Owners puts the first piece at January 31 and the second at July 31, though a local government can set another schedule. Let five working days pass after January 31 without the first payment and everything still unpaid becomes delinquent February 1. Paying a City of Milwaukee bill

Special charges and assessments left unpaid by mid-November may be added to the tax bill. Those can't be appealed or negotiated.

Delinquent bills can be paid online, by mail or in person at the Milwaukee County Courthouse. Online payments go through Value Payment Systems, which charges 2.55 percent for credit or debit cards and a flat $1.50 for e-checks. The county gets none of that fee.

The Treasurer's records show every unpaid delinquent tax, penalty and interest charge, and a parcel with nothing owed shows a zero balance. A payment made today might not post until the next business day. If an amount looks wrong, or you want a monthly payment plan, call (414) 278-4033.

If taxes go unpaid long enough, the county can use in rem foreclosure, which moves title to a delinquent property under Wisconsin law. The county doesn't sell foreclosed properties for the back taxes. It sells them at fair market value like any other property. Lender foreclosure auctions are a separate matter, held by the Sheriff on Monday mornings, and the Sheriff advises buyers to check for delinquent taxes first.

If back taxes are what stands between you and a sale, a cash buyer can often close without waiting on a lender's appraisal, and the payoff comes out of the proceeds at closing. Ask the Treasurer for the exact amount owed on your closing date, since the 18 percent yearly charge keeps growing the balance until it is paid.

After the sale

Buyers record their deed through the Milwaukee County Register of Deeds. When the old owner's name is still printed on a city bill, the buyer ticks the change-of-address box on the coupon, which keeps any refund check from going to the seller. Chippewa County in brief

West-central Wisconsin is home to Chippewa County, part of the Eau Claire metro area, with Chippewa Falls as its seat and biggest city. Residents numbered 66,297 in 2020 and about 67,614 by the 2025 estimate.

Most housing is owner-occupied: 28,688 units in 2020, with 8.4% vacant, and 73.7% of occupied homes owned. Some 62.5% of people live in rural areas. A listing might be a city house in Chippewa Falls or a farmhouse on acreage, and the tax questions are different for each.

Places that bill property tax include:

  • Cities: Bloomer, Chippewa Falls, Cornell, Stanley (partly in Clark County) and the part of Eau Claire inside Chippewa County.
  • Villages: Boyd, Cadott, Lake Hallie and New Auburn (partly in Barron County).
  • Unincorporated places such as Holcombe, Jim Falls and Lake Wissota.

Who collects the tax

Payments go first to a local treasurer, and the Chippewa County Treasurer picks up whatever is left later. For the current year, anything paid in December or January belongs with the town, village or city treasurer.

At the county level, the treasurer's office receives all postponed and delinquent real estate tax, settles accounts with the taxing districts, maintains the lottery credit file and property listing, prepares the assessment and tax rolls, prints the bills, handles tax deeds and answers questions about values, legal descriptions and tax information. Unclaimed funds are held there too.

The treasurer's web pages give owners several tools:

  • Current mill rates and credits.
  • Lottery credit FAQs and forms.
  • A Property Owners Guide in PDF form.
  • An assessor list and a list of local treasurer addresses and phone numbers.
  • Online tax lookup and payment through the county's public portal.

The rates and credits are posted every year, so look there before estimating what you owe.

Due dates and penalties

The whole bill or the first installment is due January 31, and the second installment is due July 31. A missed first date makes the entire unpaid balance delinquent.

For a seller, the practical point is timing. If you list in the spring, the first installment has probably been paid and the second is still ahead, so the closing agent can split the balance between you and the buyer. If you list after July 31, ask whether both installments were paid before you sign a listing agreement.

Appealing your assessment

Start with the Board of Review for your own town, village or city. It holds a hearing and then decides. Wisconsin Statute 70.47 governs, and the only local part is the calendar.

Each year the board gathers within 45 days of the fourth Monday of April, after the clerk has posted a notice at least 15 days in advance. As the owner you will need:

  • Notice to the clerk, spoken or written, 48 hours or more ahead of the opening meeting.
  • A written objection delivered inside the first two hours of that meeting, using a form if the board asks for one.
  • Your own view of what the land and the improvements are worth, with the facts that back it up.
  • A willingness to give testimony under oath. A phone hearing or sworn written statements may be allowed.

Proof is your job. The assessor's figure is presumed right until you show otherwise. Members vote by roll call, and tied votes leave the assessment alone. An owner who turns down the assessor's reasonable certified-mail request to look at the outside of the property can forfeit the right to appear. Ask your municipal clerk, not the county, for the meeting date.

Selling with taxes owed

You need three things: the balance, an agreement on who pays what at closing, and a recorded deed with a transfer return. A house with tax owing can close as long as the payoff is lined up.

  • Call the Chippewa County Treasurer for the parcel's balance, which includes interest at the delinquent-account rate.
  • Learn whether the first installment reached the local treasurer and whether July 31 is still open.
  • Instruct the closing agent to take the tax out of your proceeds.
  • Budget for the state transfer fee, which the Register of Deeds collects when the deed is recorded. Wisconsin Statute 77.22 sets it at 30 cents per $100 of value or fraction, paid by the grantor.

Inherited property often goes this route. A transfer by will, descent or survivorship is exempt under Statute 77.25(11), and parent-to-child transfers for little or no payment are exempt under 77.25(8). Even then, the return shows the value and the exemption number.

The steps are identical for a house in Chippewa Falls, Bloomer or Lake Hallie and a farm near Cadott or Cornell. Only the local treasurer differs.

Local demand

Work in and around Chippewa Falls and the wider Eau Claire area is what pulls most buyers in. The county has gained population in every census since 1990, rising from 52,360 that year to 55,195 in 2000, 62,415 in 2010 and 66,297 in 2020.

The result for a seller is a steady market near the cities and a thinner one on big rural parcels. Whatever the parcel, confirm which town, village or city treasurer takes the January payment.

What to gather before you list

A short folder of papers saves time once a buyer appears. Cash buyers move fast, and the delays usually come from missing tax or deed paperwork.

  • Your latest tax bill, which shows the parcel, the assessor's value, the credits and the municipality.
  • Proof of what you have paid so far, including whether the first installment went to the local treasurer.
  • A payoff figure from the County Treasurer if any installment is late.
  • The names of everyone who owns the property, which matters on the transfer return and for inherited homes.
  • A note of any exemption you plan to claim, with its statute number.

Choosing a cash sale does not skip the deed or the transfer return, because both are still required. It removes the buyer's loan approval, so the tax payoff is often the last open item.

Frequently asked questions

When are Chippewa County property taxes due?

The full bill or first installment is due January 31, and the second installment July 31. The first payment goes to the local treasurer and the second to the Chippewa County Treasurer.

What interest rate does Chippewa County charge for late taxes?

1% per month. A missed first installment starts it February 1 on the unpaid balance, and a missed July 31 payment carries 1% a month reaching back to February 1.

Where do I pay delinquent Chippewa County property tax?

Pay it to the Chippewa County Treasurer. All delinquent tax is paid there, not to the local treasurer.

Who handles property tax

The county treasurer is the main office. Additional fees can apply, so ask for a final payoff.

At the state level, Wis. Stat. 74.47 sets the floor at one percent per month or part of one, and a county board may add up to 0.5 percent monthly by ordinance.

Look up bills, due dates and a future-dated payoff on the city's website. Fees there: $1.50 per e-check, 1.5 percent on debit and 2.40 percent on credit, each card type with a $2.00 minimum. Delinquent taxes from earlier years belong to the county treasurer, 715-346-1348. Spot a star under the parcel number on your bill? That marks a prior year delinquency.

Stat. 70.47 the board clerk needs your notice of intent 48 hours before the board first meets, and your written objection is due in that meeting's first two hours, unless good cause waives the notice.

Assessors are listed by town, village and city, so the municipal clerk is the right first call.

Selling with taxes owed

Identify the office that holds your bill and request its payoff figure before you pick a closing date. In Stevens Point you deal with the city on current taxes and the county on delinquent ones. In most other places the second installment sits with the county treasurer.

The county's two installments land on January 31 and July 31. Stevens Point runs three, on January 31, April 30 and July 31. Reminders aren't mailed, so note the dates yourself.

To the county treasurer on Church Street, with exceptions: the City of Stevens Point, the Towns of Almond, Belmont and Lanark, and the Village of Milladore. The towns and village use their own treasurer for the first installment, and the city for every current one.

Unpaid on September 1 triggers a tax certificate and starts a two-year window to pay. If it isn't paid by then, the county forecloses by tax deed.

School district and municipal levies make up much of the bill, so check with the local clerk which ones apply to your parcel.

Due dates

Your local treasurer gets the first installment, or the entire bill, by January 31. The county Treasurer gets the second by July 31. A rule trips up many owners: an installment must arrive within five working days of its due date, otherwise the whole unpaid balance turns delinquent.

Section E of the form asks about taxes, special assessments and permits, so pull together your latest tax bill, any special assessment notices and your permit records beforehand.

Steps in order: get the payoff, confirm which installments are paid, collect your permit and assessment papers, finish the condition report, and deliver it to the buyer on time after the contract is accepted. A late report gives the buyer a short window to rescind.

When you call the Treasurer's office, have the parcel number and the property address ready, and note the name of the person who gives you the figure. Keep the written payoff with your closing file. If the second installment is still open and the sale will close before July 31, decide in the contract who pays it, and ask the title company to show that split on the closing statement. Sellers with a delinquent parcel should ask the same office how interest is counted through the expected closing date.

A cash buyer may close sooner, yet the tax balance and the disclosure duties are identical.

Who collects Sauk County property tax?

Local treasurers take the first installment or full payment, due January 31. The county Treasurer, at 505 Broadway, Room 148, Baraboo, takes July 31 second installments and every delinquent payment.

Go to Ascent Land Records, linked from the Treasurer page. Fees are 2.50% for credit cards, $2.95 for debit cards and $1.50 for e-checks up to $10,000. Delton, Fairfield, Greenfield and Sumpter also take first installments there.

Interest and penalty of 1.5% are added on the first of every month until the balance is paid. Paying an installment later than five working days after its due date turns the whole remainder delinquent.

Does the county set my Sauk County assessed value?

No, that belongs to your town, village or city assessor. Disputes start with the assessor and move to the municipal Board of Review, which meets within 45 days of the fourth Monday in April.

Yes, anything unpaid is cleared at or before closing. The Treasurer can tell you the balance, and the title company pays it from your proceeds. Chapter 709 also requires a condition report unless you qualify for an exemption.

Who does what

Two layers of government share the job here. Every town, village and city in Calumet County contracts with its own assessor and has its own treasurer. The county treasurer's office in Chilton, at 206 Court Street, takes care of the county's part. Walk in Monday through Friday between 8 am and 4:30 pm, or call (920) 849-1457.

That office accepts every delinquent or postponed real estate payment for the county, collects the first installment for the City of New Holstein, settles the rolls with towns, villages, cities and school districts, sends out delinquent notices and processes parcels that become eligible for tax foreclosure.

A Real Property Lister sits in the same building. After a sale, the Transfer Form recorded at the Register of Deeds is forwarded to the treasurer's office, and that is how the owner and mailing details on the parcel get changed. The lister also assembles the tax rolls for the municipal assessors, whose values generally come in between late February and late May.

Selling in a farm-heavy county

This is a small, largely rural county with Lake Winnebago on its western side, and Chilton is the seat. The 2020 count was 52,442 people, and the current estimate is 53,982. It falls within the Appleton metro area, and bits of Appleton, Kaukauna and Menasha extend into the northwest.

Farmland is taxed differently. Agricultural acreage is valued for what it can produce, which is why a farm parcel can carry a zero estimated market value on its bill. Sellers with acreage should read the bill carefully before a buyer asks about numbers.

When property taxes are due

You can pay everything by January 31 or split the bill, with the second half due July 31. Local treasurers mail real and personal property bills in early to mid December.

Splitting is open on any bill over $100. The first half goes to the local treasurer by January 31 and the second half to the Calumet County Treasurer by July 31. The first half must be paid in full and on time or the installment option is lost. Personal property tax is paid to the local treasurer in full by January 31 unless the bill shows an installment option.

Taxing districts and credits

A bill can include up to five main districts: the State of Wisconsin, Calumet County, a technical college, your municipality and a school district. Some parcels also fall in a special district for a lake, sewer or fire protection, and that district takes a share as well.

  • School districts: Appleton, Brillion, Chilton, Hilbert, Kaukauna, Kiel, Kimberly, Menasha, New Holstein, Stockbridge and Wrightstown.

Two credits can lower the bill. The first dollar credit goes to any property with a structure on it, whatever its use or value. Appealing your assessment

Because Calumet County assessors answer to individual towns, villages and cities, the Board of Review that hears your case sits in the municipality where your house is.

The timetable comes from Wisconsin Statute 70.47. A 45-day window opens on the fourth Monday of April, and the clerk posts a notice at least 15 days ahead (30 days when the municipality is revaluing). Move quickly:

  • Dispute the total of land plus improvements. Land alone or buildings alone cannot be challenged.
  • Put your own value in writing with supporting facts, and be prepared to testify under oath.

An assessor's value is presumed correct, and a tied vote leaves it standing. Beyond the board, an excessive assessment claim under Statute 74.37 is the next option. Ask your municipal clerk for this year's meeting date.

Unpaid property tax

Late tax turns delinquent, the interest and penalty keep growing, and eventually the county may foreclose. Where you pay depends on the kind of tax: delinquent real property tax goes to the Calumet County Treasurer and delinquent personal property tax goes to your local treasurer.

Interest and penalty run 1.5% a month from February 1, with notices mailed in February and August. A parcel that reaches the foreclosure-eligible stage is processed by the treasurer. If you own one, phone the office to see where it stands and whether a county tax auction is coming.

Selling is easier before foreclosure than after it. Get a payoff figure early and settle the account at closing.

Selling with taxes owed

Ask the treasurer for the exact balance, then clear it through closing. What you owe depends on which installment has been paid, so last December's bill is only a starting point.

  • Call the Calumet County Treasurer at (920) 849-1457 and ask for the full amount owed on the parcel, interest and penalty included.
  • Confirm whether the first installment reached the local treasurer and whether the July 31 installment is still open.
  • Give the closing agent the parcel details so unpaid tax comes out of your sale proceeds.
  • Have the deed recorded at the Register of Deeds with the electronic transfer return. Under Statute 77.22(1) the grantor pays 30 cents per $100 of value or fraction, collected at recording.
  • After recording, the Real Property Lister changes the billing name and address on the parcel.

A house with a delinquent balance can still sell. The title work and the payoff only need to line up, which is easier when the tax figure is known early. A cash buyer skips the lender's review, though the tax payoff is still part of the closing.

January 31 for the full bill or the first installment, and July 31 for the second installment. The first goes to your local treasurer and the second to the Calumet County Treasurer in Chilton.

What interest does Calumet County charge on late property tax?

The rate is 1.5% per month, counted from February 1. It applies to a late first or second installment once the unpaid tax is delinquent.

Who sets the value of my Calumet County home?

A municipal assessor does. Each town, village and city hires its own, and values go to the county's Real Property Lister, usually between late February and late May. The state separately estimates fair market value from arm's length sales for the bill.

Can I pay my Calumet County tax bill in two parts?

Yes, if the bill is over $100. Pay the first half to the local treasurer by January 31 to keep the option, and the second half to the county treasurer by July 31. A late first payment ends the installment option.

The first dollar credit and the lottery and gaming credit. The first goes to any property with a structure, and the second to property used as the owner's primary residence.

Under Wis. Stat. 74.11(7), a first installment that the proper official has not received within five working days of January 31 leaves the whole remaining balance delinquent from February 1. Delinquent real property tax is payable to the county treasurer, with interest and penalties running from the preceding February 1. The simple fix is to pay online or to mail with days to spare. When tax bills arrive

December is bill season. Wis. Stat. 74.09(5) sets the third Monday in December as the mailing limit for each taxing district clerk, after levies come in by December 1. Under 74.09(6), a bill that goes missing leaves the tax, and the collection of delinquent amounts, unchanged. If yours has not appeared by the holidays, call your municipal clerk.

New owner by purchase or inheritance? Ask the treasurer to verify the parcel number and the installments already received before you send money.

Who sets and reviews assessments?

Values come from local assessors, and objections go to your municipality's board of review. Under Wis. Stat. 70.46, the default town board of review is the supervisors plus the clerk; a city or village board is the mayor or president, the clerk and any officers the governing body appoints. Parcel listing and mapping belong to the county's Real Property Lister Office, which also links the county with the Wisconsin Department of Revenue. Its hours are Monday through Thursday, 7:00 a.m. to 5:30 p.m.

Your bill combines levies from several taxing bodies, and Wis. Stat. 74.09(3) makes it list the school district tax, each other jurisdiction's tax, the credits and the change from last year. Read those lines first. They show whether an appeal is worth the effort.

How a board of review hearing works

The hearing is formal and sworn, and you carry the burden. The main rules in Wis. Stat. 70.47:

  • Sessions happen once a year across 45 days starting the fourth Monday of April.
  • Notice of your intent to object is due 48 hours or more before the first meeting, though good cause can earn a limited waiver.
  • Hand the clerk your written objection in the opening two hours of that meeting.
  • Put your estimate of land value and of improvement value on paper, with the information behind it.
  • The assessor's number holds unless you prove it wrong.
  • Votes are taken by roll call; a tie keeps the assessment.

Phone appearances and sworn written statements may be allowed in place of showing up. Clerks retain the records for seven years or longer, so copies can be requested. Turn down a reasonable certified-mail request from the assessor to see the outside of the property, and you give up the right to appear.

Lottery and gaming credit

The credit cuts the bill of a Wisconsin resident who owns a dwelling and lived in it as the primary residence on January 1 of the levy year. Nothing happens automatically. Apply to the county treasurer for the county where the property lies, or to the city treasurer when the city collects taxes under Wis. Stat. 74.87.

When the bill is missing it, apply to the town, village or city treasurer by the next January 31. Late claims go to the Department of Revenue, due October 1 following the bill. You get one primary residence only, and these do not count:

  • Rental units
  • Vacant land
  • Garages
  • Business property

A hospital stay or other absence of about six months or less does not change which home is your residence.

Selling a Washington County house

West Bend is the seat of a county in the Milwaukee metro area, just north of Waukesha County. The 2020 count showed 136,761 residents and 58,311 housing units, 4.2 percent of them vacant, and 77.3 percent of occupied homes were owner-occupied.

With an inherited or tenant-occupied house, get the parcel's tax history from the county treasurer before picking a closing date. Pass the payment record to the closing agent so the settlement statement shows what is paid and what remains. When a bill is outstanding, the treasurer can quote a payoff. Cash buyers can often work to your timetable, a plus when an estate or a tax balance is involved. Also note where each payment went, because January payments went to the municipality while later ones went to the county.

Taxes owed at closing

Selling with a balance is routine. Ask the treasurer for the payoff on the exact parcel, since delinquent amounts carry interest and penalties from the preceding February 1. Give that figure to the closing agent, who can pay it from your proceeds at the table. If the second installment is not yet due, the closing agent and the buyer will typically divide the year's tax between you, pegged to the closing date, so have your payment record ready. A short phone call to the treasurer a week before closing confirms nothing has changed. Keep copies of any receipts or online confirmations; they settle questions quickly if a payment seems to be missing from the county's records.

When are Washington County property taxes due?

Two dates: January 31 for the first half or the full amount, July 31 for the second half. Municipal treasurer through January 31, county treasurer afterward.

What does a card payment add to the cost?

Credit cards add 2.5 percent, debit cards $3.50 and e-checks $1.50. The fee rides on top of the tax, and the total is displayed before you submit.

Will a mailed payment count if I mail it on January 30?

Possibly not. Regional sorting centers now apply postmarks, so a stamp can lag your mailing by days. The county treasurer recommends paying online or mailing sooner.

Who qualifies for the lottery and gaming credit?

Wisconsin residents who own a home and occupy it as their primary residence on January 1 of the levy year, provided they apply. Rentals, vacant land and garages are out.

How do I appeal my assessment?

Tell the municipal board of review 48 hours or more before its opening meeting, then file a written objection during the meeting's first two hours. Its 45-day window opens the fourth Monday of April.

Barron County housing and who collects

Barron County is in northwestern Wisconsin, with the city of Barron as county seat. The 2020 census counted 46,711 residents, about 78 percent of them in rural areas, and 73.2 percent of occupied homes were owner-occupied. The cities are Barron, Chetek, Cumberland and Rice Lake. The villages are Almena, Cameron, Dallas, Haugen, New Auburn, Prairie Farm and Turtle Lake. Each of those places, and each surrounding town, has its own treasurer who takes first-installment payments.

Which Barron County office handles my property tax?

The county office to know is the Barron County Treasurer and Real Property Lister, at 335 E Monroe Ave, Room 2412, Barron, WI 54812-1478. Weekday hours run 8 a.m. until 4:30 p.m., and callers reach the staff at 715-537-6280. The Real Property Lister side maintains the parcel descriptions behind the assessment and tax roll, drawing on records from the Register of Deeds, surveying, zoning and mapping, the assessor and the treasurer. The office also hosts the online tax data portal.

The dates come from state law. Wis. Stat. 74.11 gives you a choice between one full payment and two equal installments, due January 31 and July 31. A parcel with a total bill under $100 is paid whole by January 31. Payments on or before January 31 are sent to the town, village or city treasurer, and the county treasurer takes everything later. Assessment is local in Wisconsin, so your municipal clerk can tell you who assessed your parcel and when the local Board of Review meets.

How late payments work

Interest and penalty are counted back to February 1. The county posts the rate as 1 percent interest plus a half percent penalty each month, 1.5 percent in all, in line with the interest authority in Wis. Stat. 74.47. The county gives 10.5 percent as the August charge on 2025 taxes still unpaid after the July 31, 2026 installment date. Taxes for 2025 come due in 2026 because they follow the prior year's assessment.

Miss the first installment and the full unpaid balance is delinquent from February 1. Mail timing deserves attention:

  • The postmark on a mailed check must be dated no later than the due date.
  • Local mail is often postmarked in Saint Paul, Minnesota, sometimes days later, so carry the envelope to the local post office and ask for a hand stamp.
  • An envelope that arrives with no postmark cannot be treated as timely.

Counties and municipalities can also sue an owner to recover delinquent taxes that came due while that person owned the property. This normally follows approval by the county board or governing body, and it is limited to the amount owed plus interest and penalties.

The bill lists the tax from each taxing jurisdiction for the previous and current year with the percentage change, shows the school district tax net of the state credit, includes a notice of available credits, and says whether delinquent taxes or special assessments are attached to the parcel.

Read that last line before you list a house. It is the quickest way to spot a past-due amount. These bill requirements come from Wis. Stat. 74.09, next to the payment rules in chapter 74.

Assessment objections run on a different clock. What a Barron County seller owes at closing

On a sale the seller owes Wisconsin's transfer fee of 30 cents for every $100 of value, and the register of deeds takes it at recording. The grantor and grantee both sign an electronic transfer return first. The fee comes from Wis. Stat. 77.22, and exemptions in section 77.25 cover cases such as conveyances by will or descent, foreclosure deeds, deeds in lieu of foreclosure to the lender and transfers between a parent and child for little or no payment. A conveyance claiming an exemption must state the reason on its face.

Property tax is its own matter. Request a statement of any delinquent amount from the Barron County Treasurer. Separately, ask the title company how the current year will be divided between you and the buyer. Paying the delinquent amount with interest and any penalty clears the debt, provided no tax certificate has yet been issued. Because first-installment payments go to the municipal treasurer, confirm with that treasurer which installment has been paid.

Getting ready to sell

A short checklist keeps a Barron County closing from stalling on tax paperwork.

  • Find the tax bill and check its last line for delinquent taxes or special assessments.
  • Learn which municipal treasurer took your January payment and whether the second installment is paid.
