  • If land was divided during the year, ask the municipal treasurer about a bill split before January 15.

Cash buyers often close faster since no lender underwriting is involved. The transfer return and the tax payoff still apply, so build both into your timeline.

When are Barron County property taxes due?

The first installment, or the entire bill, is due January 31, and the second installment July 31. A bill under $100 is paid whole by January 31. Money paid on or before that date goes to the local municipal treasurer.

What interest applies to late Barron County taxes?

Each month costs 1.5 percent, counted from February 1: one percent in interest and half a percent in penalty. The county gives 10.5 percent as the August figure for 2025 taxes.

How do I contact the Barron County Treasurer?

Call 715-537-6280 or visit Room 2412 at 335 E Monroe Ave in Barron, weekdays between 8 a.m. and 4:30 p.m. Mail goes to Barron County Treasurer's Office, 335 E Monroe Ave Rm 2412, Barron, WI 54812-1478.

Who covers the transfer fee on a Barron County sale?

The seller. Sellers pay 30 cents per $100 of value, and the register of deeds takes the money at recording. Inheritance transfers, foreclosure deeds and certain family transfers for little or no payment are exempt.

What if my lottery credit is missing from my Barron County tax bill?

Ask your municipal treasurer to take a late claim, which must be in by January 31. Only an owner-occupied primary residence qualifies, and the Treasurer's Office can answer questions about eligibility.

Which office to call

Your municipal treasurer takes the first payment, and after January 31 the La Crosse County Treasurer handles it. The county office is in the Administration Center at 212 6th Street North, La Crosse, WI 54601. Call (608) 785-9711, write to treasurer@lacrossecounty.org, or stop by Monday to Friday, 8:00 am to 4:30 pm.

The dividing rule is Wis. Stat. 74.11(6). Money in by January 31 stays with the taxation district treasurer, and every other payment is the county's. For the amount of a first installment, ask the treasurer of your city, village or town. After the first deadline, call the county.

Assessments are a separate job. The county's Zoning and Land Information office keeps parcel records and the public property portal (608-785-9722), but the municipal assessor sets the values. County staff must carry the assessor's numbers and cannot change them, so a disagreement goes to the assessor first.

Due dates

One option is the whole bill by January 31. The other is two installments, one due January 31 and one due July 31. Wis. Stat. 74.11(2) allows two installments, unless the real property tax on a parcel totals under $100, in which case it is due in full by January 31. A municipality can adopt a three-installment ordinance under 74.12, so ask your local treasurer if your bill has more than two payment slips.

Neither 2027 date is a business day. January 31, 2027 is a Sunday, which stretches the five-working-day window to Friday, February 5, 2027 (74.11(7)(b)). July 31, 2027 is a Saturday, and its window runs to Friday, August 6, 2027 (74.11(8)(b)). Mailing early is still the safer choice. Section 74.69(1) treats a postmarked payment as timely when it reaches the right official within five business days of the due date.

Late payment cost

A late bill is charged 1.5 percent monthly on what is unpaid, and the installment option disappears. The 1 percent is from Wis. Stat. 74.47(1), and La Crosse County Ordinance 4.05 adds the 0.5 percent penalty that 74.47(2) allows. Each is counted per month or fraction of a month, reaching back to February 1.

A few rules control what happens next:

  • Miss the first installment deadline and the full remaining balance is delinquent from February 1 (74.11(7)).
  • Delinquent real property tax, with interest and penalty, is paid to the county treasurer (74.11(11)).
  • A short payment is applied in a fixed order under 74.12(11)(a): personal property taxes first, then delinquent utility charges, special charges, special assessments and special taxes, with real property tax last.
  • Treasurers cannot waive interest for hardship. The only exceptions are a severe postal error and active military deployment of 90 days or more.

If you cannot cover an installment, pay what you can by the deadline and keep paying every month. Because of the application order, a partial payment may go to a special charge before it reaches the tax itself.

Reading your tax bill

Four main jurisdictions appear on the bill: the county, the school district, the technical college and your municipality. A parcel inside a lake district or sanitary district carries that district's share too. The net assessed value rate is the combined mill rate of every jurisdiction, applied to your total assessed value, and the product is your tax before the lottery credit.

The estimated fair market value on the bill is calculated by the Department of Revenue from arm's-length sales in the past year. It is not an appraisal and not a prediction of your sale price. The average assessment ratio compares your municipality's assessed values with market value. Land and improvements are taxed at the same rate even when their values differ, and state law requires recently passed referenda to be listed.

No bill by December 21? Call your municipal treasurer. A missing bill does not stop interest from running (74.09(6)).

Appealing your assessment

Your municipality's assessor is the first stop, and the municipal Board of Review is the second. In the City of La Crosse, the Assessor's Office is at 608-789-7525 (assessor@cityoflacrosse.org), and the City Clerk's Office at 608-789-7510 takes Board of Review filings. The city says an informal review answers most questions. If you still disagree, let the city clerk know, in writing or by voice, 48 hours or more before the board opens, then file an approved objection form before or within the first two hours of the first meeting.

The city calls its Board of Review a quasi-judicial body of five appointed residents that works like a court. It weighs the facts offered at the hearing, and the owner must show the property is assessed unfairly compared with the general level of assessment in the district. The calendar comes from state law, with sessions held in the 45 days starting the fourth Monday of April (70.47(1)).

A court can review the board's decision by certiorari, filed within 90 days after the decision notice (70.47(13)). Outside the city, ask the village or town clerk for the schedule.

Ownership records and selling

Names on a tax bill come from recorded documents at the Register of Deeds, so ownership problems show up on the bill first. The county's Real Property FAQ gives several practical rules:

  • After a divorce, the former spouse's name stays on bills and notices until a recorded document, such as a quit claim deed or divorce judgment, changes title.
  • When an owner dies, a parcel held in joint tenancy or as survivorship marital property is cleared with a Termination of Decedent's Interest form filed at the Register of Deeds. Other kinds of title may call for an attorney and probate.
  • A parcel split during the year is billed as a whole to the owner at the time of the split, and the new parcels are assessed and taxed the next year. Assessments describe the property as of January 1.
  • Mailing address changes go through the municipal treasurer or the county office.
  • The public portal searches by owner name, address, parcel number or tax bill number, and the parcel format is ##-#####-### with zeros filled in.

If the contract is silent on taxes at delivery of the deed, Wis. Stat. 74.15 supplies the split. The seller owes the buyer one-twelfth of last year's tax for each month before the deed, and the sale month too when the deed lands after the 15th. For a payoff on delinquent tax, call the County Treasurer. Selling for cash leaves this untouched; the payoff is still taken from the proceeds at closing.

Credits for homeowners

Three state programs can lower what an owner pays. The Lottery Credit is meant for Wisconsin homeowners who occupied the home as their primary residence on January 1, and you apply through the Department of Revenue. Completed applications reach the county monthly. If you claim after the first installment date, upload a copy or photo of your latest tax bill before October 1. Once granted, the credit remains until the owner or the department removes it.

The Homestead Credit is filed with state income taxes and helps lower-income owners. Disabled service members and surviving spouses can ask the County service office about a separate state property tax credit. Owners who struggle to pay can also talk with the County Treasurer about monthly payments, because smaller regular payments reduce the interest that builds up.

La Crosse County for sellers

La Crosse County is the most populous county on Wisconsin's western border, with Minnesota across the river. The city of La Crosse is the seat. The county has two cities, La Crosse and Onalaska, and villages including Bangor, Holmen, Rockland and West Salem.

Population is 121,339 and there are 55,407 housing units. Owners occupy about 62.2 percent of homes. The median home value is $257,000, median gross rent is $1,059 and median household income is $73,013. Winters are cold, with January highs averaging 25.9 degrees, so heating costs and roof condition are fair topics for a buyer's inspection.

Frequently asked questions

When are La Crosse County property taxes due?

Either the full amount by January 31 or two payments, January 31 and July 31. Your municipal treasurer receives payments through January 31, and the La Crosse County Treasurer receives later ones.

How much interest does La Crosse County charge on late taxes?

1 percent monthly under Wis. Stat. 74.47, plus a 0.5 percent monthly penalty from county ordinance 4.05, all counted from February 1. A treasurer cannot waive it for hardship.

Where is the La Crosse County Treasurer's office?

Inside the Administration Center, 212 6th Street North, La Crosse, WI 54601. Call (608) 785-9711. It is staffed weekdays from 8:00 am until 4:30 pm.

Who can change my property assessment in La Crosse County?

Only your municipal assessor and, on appeal, the municipal Board of Review. The county's land information office maintains the values the assessor sets. In the City of La Crosse, call the Assessor's Office at 608-789-7525.

How do I remove a deceased spouse's name from a La Crosse County tax bill?

For a home owned in joint tenancy or as survivorship marital property, the Register of Deeds takes a Termination of Decedent's Interest form. For other ownership types an attorney may have to transfer title, possibly in probate.

Lottery and gaming credit

Owners who occupy the house as a primary residence on January 1 may get the Wisconsin lottery and gaming credit off the bill. It is not available on rentals, vacant land or garages. If your bill omits it, apply at the municipal treasurer's office by January 31, or file late with the Department of Revenue by October 1.

A cabin or second home is ineligible. At a sale the credit stays attached to the parcel, so include it when you prorate, and an occupying buyer submits a new application.

What happens when taxes are not paid?

Vilas County goes after delinquent property through an in rem tax foreclosure, carried out by the county treasurer. If you owe, the balance can usually be paid out of closing proceeds, and Wis. Stat. 74.51 lets anyone discharge delinquent real property taxes, with interest and any penalty, before a tax certificate issues.

Wis. Stat. 74.49 allows partial payments of $20 or more on delinquent taxes. Late payments are accepted year-round, so you can bring an account current whenever you like. Request a written payoff valid through your closing date.

Vilas is northern lake country whose market runs on tourism and second homes. Population is 23,761 (2025 estimate), up 3.1% since April 2020, with 37.1% of residents 65 or older. Median home value among owners is $300,000, and 84.0% of housing units are owner-occupied. Households number 11,147 against 25,498 housing units, which points to seasonal use.

Lake cottages often sell on a different schedule than town houses. A winter closing can complicate access and inspections, and the July installment still comes due, so discuss all three with your agent or buyer.

What to ask before you list

Get the parcel's tax history, and any delinquency, from the treasurer. Have the Real Property Listing office confirm the name and mailing address on the parcel. Renting to vacationers? The county website carries a Tourist Rooming Houses page under its Business menu, and the county can tell you what approval, if any, passes to a buyer. Check before promising that the rental income transfers.

Gather what the title company will ask for: the newest bill, proof of payments and, if money is owed, a written payoff. With a cash buyer no lender reviews these items, yet title work still verifies them before closing.

A workable order of operations: confirm the January payment went to the right local treasurer, pull the bill history from the lookup tool, ask the county treasurer for a payoff if anything is delinquent, and hand all of it to the closing agent. If the second installment is not yet due when you close, expect it to be prorated between you and the buyer. Keep your parcel number on every request, since both county offices search by it.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I pay my first installment in Vilas County?

Locally: the town treasurer, or the City of Eagle River. On-time first-half and full payments are made there, while the county takes July money and late payments.

What is the Vilas County Treasurer's address and phone?

The office sits at 330 Court Street, Eagle River, WI 54521, and answers at 715-479-3609. It is open weekdays 8:00 AM to 4:00 PM; holiday closings appear on the county website.

Can I pay Vilas County taxes online?

Yes, for second installments and delinquent taxes, through Point and Pay. Cards cost 2.39% and electronic checks cost $1.50. First installments go to your local municipality, which can say whether it offers an online option.

How is the Vilas County foreclosure process different?

The county uses an in rem tax foreclosure, run by the county treasurer. An owner in arrears can discharge the taxes with interest before a tax certificate issues.

Does the lottery credit carry to the buyer of a Vilas County home?

Yes, it stays with the parcel and belongs in the proration. A buyer who moves in as a primary resident files a fresh application.

Where to send your payment

Mail or bring the first payment to your town or village treasurer. Payments made after July 31 are sent to the Burnett County Treasurer instead. Your local treasurer's name and address sit at the top left of the bill.

Section 74.11(6) draws the line: anything paid by January 31 goes to the local taxation district, and everything else goes to the county. So current-year real estate tax paid through January goes to the town or village, and what is paid after July 31 goes to Burnett County.

No city exists inside the county. Its 24 municipalities are 21 towns (Anderson, Blaine, Daniels, Dewey, Grantsburg, Jackson, LaFollette, Lincoln, Meenon, Oakland, Roosevelt, Rusk, Sand Lake, Scott, Siren, Swiss, Trade Lake, Union, Webb Lake, West Marshland and Wood River) and three villages (Grantsburg, Siren and Webster). Because Grantsburg and Siren are both a town and a village, look at the bill to see which payee applies before you write the check.

Due dates and penalties

Tax comes due January 31. You can pay everything then or split the bill, with the second half due July 31 (s. 74.11(2)). Small bills, under $100, can not be split and are due in full by January 31.

  • Miss January 31 by more than five working days and the full unpaid balance is delinquent from February 1.
  • Miss July 31 by more than five working days and the remaining balance is delinquent from August 1.
  • If either date lands on a weekend, you have until close of business on the first Friday of the following month.

The calendar matters in 2027. January 31 is a Sunday, which makes Friday, February 5, 2027 the last on-time day. July 31 is a Saturday, so the July cutoff slides to Friday, August 6, 2027.

Late real estate tax is paid at the county treasurer's office, with interest and penalties counted from the previous February 1. A municipality can also pass an ordinance for three or more payments, the first half due by April 30 and the balance by July 31 (s. 74.12). Your bill, or a call to your local treasurer, shows which plan covers your parcel.

Address changes and payment alerts

The Real Property Lister handles changes to the name and mailing address on a bill. Call 715.349.2183.

Records are being moved to Ascent Land Records software, and the treasurer's page lets you enroll in text or email alerts. The four alerts are a bill ready, a payment receipted, a postponement reminder and delinquent tax due. Out-of-state owners of seasonal or inherited property get the most from these, because a bill mailed to a stale address is easy to miss.

The treasurer's office also sends delinquent notices and postponed-tax reminders, issues tax certificates, runs the Lottery and Gaming Credit and prepares the tax settlements.

Assessments and how to appeal

The assessor for your town or village decides your value, and the county copies it onto the roll. A disagreement starts with a call to that assessor, whose name is on your municipality's page of the county website.

The next step is the local Board of Review, which meets in a 45-day period beginning the fourth Monday of April (s. 70.47). Town boards consist of the supervisors and clerk unless the town has created another board by ordinance, and village boards use the president and clerk. One member at least must complete state training each year.

  • Let the board clerk know you plan to object, in writing or orally, no later than 48 hours before the first meeting.
  • Submit the written objection within two hours of the meeting's start. Department of Revenue form PA-115A is used.
  • Prepare your own value for the land and the improvements and the facts that support it.
  • Assume the board starts from the assessor's figure and moves only for evidence.

Still unhappy? A court appeal by certiorari has a 90-day clock from the notice of the decision. Or file an excessive assessment claim with the municipality under s. 74.37 by January 31 of the year the tax is payable. The state's Guide for Property Owners covers both routes.

Two small facts help when you search. The long parcel number on a tax statement has 24 digits and starts with 07-. Owner and parcel records can be looked up on the county's Beacon mapping site.

Tax-delinquent land

The County Treasurer issues tax certificates and applications for tax deeds. Land the county takes by tax deed is sold through the county. Parcels listed on the Wisconsin Surplus online auction can be bought only through that site.

Some parcels sell over the counter at the County Clerk's office, Room 150 of the Government Center in Siren, Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Pay by cash, check or money order made out to the Burnett County Treasurer. No over-the-counter properties are for sale at this time.

If you own a parcel with unpaid taxes and want to sell it, deal with the balance first by paying or settling it with the County Treasurer.

Selling with taxes owed

A house with unpaid tax can still be sold. The title company normally pays the balance out of your proceeds at closing.

  1. Learn whether your first payment reached the town or village treasurer, and whether July 31 is still ahead.
  2. For delinquent tax, ask the County Treasurer for a payoff figure, because interest and penalties go back to February 1.
  3. Hand the title company your 24-digit parcel number so it looks up the correct record.
  4. Once the sale closes, have the Real Property Lister switch the billing address to the buyer.

With a cash buyer there is no lender review, but the tax still has to be paid off or credited at the closing table. Land that has already gone to tax deed is sold by the county, and the prior owner has no part in that sale.

Burnett County for owners and sellers

Burnett County lies in northwest Wisconsin along the Minnesota line, with Siren as its seat. It has 17,223 residents, 4.2 percent more than in 2020. Seniors 65 and up make up 35.5 percent of the population, 85.9 percent of homes are lived in by their owners, the median owner-occupied home is worth $231,300 and median household income is $62,819. Just 143 building permits were issued in 2025.

Of 15,201 housing units counted in 2020, 50.7 percent were vacant, a sign of how many are seasonal or second homes. An owner living elsewhere should turn on the bill alerts and save the Real Property Lister's number.

Frequently asked questions

Who do I pay property taxes to in Burnett County?

The first installment, due January 31, goes to your town or village treasurer. The July 31 installment and any delinquent tax go to the Burnett County Treasurer. Your local treasurer's contact details are in the upper left corner of the bill.

When are Burnett County property taxes due?

January 31 for the full bill or the first installment, and July 31 for the second. A bill under $100 must be paid in full by January 31. Once the five-working-day grace period passes, a missed first installment makes the whole balance delinquent as of February 1.

How do I change my tax bill address in Burnett County?

Call the Real Property Lister at 715.349.2183. You can also sign up on the treasurer's page for text or email alerts about new bills, receipted payments and delinquent notices.

How do I appeal my assessment in Burnett County?

Call your municipal assessor first, then go to the town or village Board of Review. Tell the clerk at least 48 hours before the first meeting and file a written objection in its first two hours. The board sits within 45 days starting the fourth Monday of April.

Does Burnett County sell tax deed land?

Yes. Land the county holds by tax deed may be listed on the Wisconsin Surplus online auction or sold over the counter at the County Clerk's office.

Who handles property tax

Several offices share the job here: town, village and city treasurers, the County Treasurer, the Real Property Lister and each municipality's Board of Review. Your location decides who gets your payment. Phillips holds the county seat and Park Falls is the biggest city, yet towns cover most of the map.

The Real Property Lister (s. 70.09) maintains parcel numbers, ownership from the most recent recorded document, mailing and property addresses, legal descriptions, assessment rolls and the figures behind each bill. If the name or mailing address on your bill is wrong, start there and with the Register of Deeds. The County Treasurer's page also has an online tax search for bills, receipts and balance-due statements, refreshed nightly.

The Price County market

Price County is large and thinly settled: 14,054 people in 2020, estimated at 13,988 for 2025, all of them rural at the 2020 count. The county has 10,735 housing units, 40.0 percent of them vacant, and 79.6 percent of occupied units are owner-occupied. That mix is one reason tax bills vary a lot from property to property. The county's tax-rate page lists Managed Forest Land acreage rates next to ordinary rates, which matters if you own timber.

Due dates and who collects

Most bills follow the state default of January 31 and July 31. Six local governments offer a third installment, and the county collects every payment for seven others. The town, city or village treasurer mails bills on or before the third Monday in December. Not getting a bill doesn't cancel the duty to pay, so call the municipal treasurer if nothing comes.

Late payments and interest

One late installment turns the entire unpaid balance delinquent, and a combined interest and penalty of 1.5 percent a month accrues from February 1. In the county's illustration, an August balance carries 10.5 percent. The treasurer can't forgive interest or penalty, because Wis. Stat. 74.47 sets the rates and state law allows relief only in narrow cases.

  • A Postal Service delay or error that made a payment arrive late can qualify for relief under s. 74.69.
  • A bankruptcy court sometimes forgives penalty when a bankruptcy is filed.
  • The treasurer takes monthly payments of $100 or more on unpaid taxes and applies them to the oldest year first.

Under s. 74.11(7), an unpaid first installment is delinquent once the five working day grace period after January 31 ends. Get an exact payoff from the treasurer before you set a closing date.

Tax foreclosure timeline

Price County uses in rem tax foreclosure, and the clock starts September 1. Any current-year bill with an unpaid balance that day gets a tax certificate. If the taxes are still unpaid two years after the certificate date, the county begins a tax deed process with a newspaper publication in April. For delinquent 2023 taxes, that publication comes in April 2027.

Title searches begin six months after publication, and the costs of publication, title search and certified mailing are added to the unpaid taxes. The timeline gives an owner behind on taxes a real window to sell, though each added fee raises the payoff. Foreclosure notices are posted on the county's In Rem and Tax Deed Notices page.

The Foundation for Rural Housing, funded partly by the Community Service Block Grant program, is listed by the treasurer for mortgage, utility and property tax help when foreclosure is underway. Call 888-400-5974.

How to appeal your assessment

The County Treasurer doesn't hear assessment appeals; the municipal Board of Review does. Section 70.47 has the clerk publish notice 15 days ahead of the first session, stretching to 30 days in a revaluation year. Boards in different towns meet on different days, so ask your clerk for the date.

  • Tell the clerk, in writing or aloud, that you plan to object. Do it 48 hours or more before the board first meets, or be ready to show good cause for missing that step.
  • Put the objection in writing during the first two hours of that meeting, unless extraordinary circumstances lead the board to waive the rule.
  • Contest land and buildings together as one value, because an owner of both can't object to only one.
  • Be ready to testify under oath and to let the assessor see the property, because refusing a reasonable written request for entry can bar you from contesting the assessment.

The county website also has an Assessors and Assessment Codes page and a revaluation primer. A higher assessed value doesn't always mean a higher bill, because what matters is how your increase compares with other properties in the community.

Credits and tax rates

Owner-occupied primary residences qualify for the lottery and gaming credit. A qualifying bill that lacks it can be fixed with a form from the County Treasurer or the Department of Revenue. The county posts its 2025 rates, payable in 2026, by municipality and school district, so a house in the City of Phillips on the Phillips district has a different rate than one in the Town of Prentice on the Prentice district.

Rates come from dividing each levy by total property value. County and school levies are apportioned to each municipality by equalized value, so a town whose values rise faster than its neighbors carries a bigger share.

Managed Forest Land owners pay an acreage rate. For entries made before 2005, open land is $0.72 per acre and closed land is $1.68. For 2005 and later, open is $1.90 and closed is $9.49. Ask the County Clerk about timber cutting notices if you are selling forest land.

The Register of Deeds

This office files and indexes deeds, easements, mortgages, satisfactions, land contracts, name changes, powers of attorney, federal tax liens, plats and certified survey maps. Documents recorded before September 1951 aren't in the searchable computer index, but the office has copies of the old grantor and grantee indexes and its tract indexes.

Staff can't draft or change a deed, give legal advice or run real estate searches. Use a real estate attorney or title company, and the State Bar of Wisconsin Lawyer Referral Service if you need to find one. Recording costs $30 plus a transfer fee of 30 cents per $100 of value, under ss. 59.43 and 77.22. The free Property Fraud Alert sends a phone or email alert when a document is recorded under your name; the support line is 800-728-3858.

Planning a sale with taxes due

Begin with the parcel's tax search record, then call the treasurer who actually collects your payments, since Price County splits collection between local offices and the county. Ask for the current balance, any special charges on the tax roll, and whether an earlier year has a tax certificate. A title company will want the same numbers.

If back taxes are building, a cash sale can close before the next fee or interest month hits, with the payoff paid from proceeds at closing. Each added publication or mailing cost makes the payoff larger, so a quick sale usually costs less than waiting.

The county also has a Surveyor's Office and a Zoning and Land Conservation office with a shoreland regulations page. Check shoreland rules with Zoning before you promise a buyer a boat house or an addition.

It depends on the municipality. The county collects every payment for the Towns of Fifield, Flambeau, Georgetown, Harmony and Worcester and the Villages of Catawba and Kennan. Elsewhere, local treasurers collect through July 31 where three installments are used.

What interest applies to late taxes?

1.5 percent per month, counted from February 1 once an installment is missed. State law sets the rate, and the treasurer can forgive interest or penalty only in narrow cases.

How long before tax foreclosure starts?

A tax certificate is issued on bills unpaid September 1. If taxes remain unpaid two years after that date, the county starts with a publication in April, and title searches follow six months later.

Where do I appeal my assessment?

To your municipal Board of Review. The clerk publishes the meeting notice, and you must give notice 48 hours ahead and file a written objection within the first two hours of the first meeting.

Can the Register of Deeds write my deed?

No. The office records documents but can't draft or change a deed or give legal advice. Use an attorney or title company, then record the signed deed with the $30 fee plus the 30 cents per $100 transfer fee.

Who collects the tax

Start with your own municipality for the first payment. Once the local deadline is behind you, the Kenosha County Treasurer is the place to pay. Find the office at 1010 56th Street, Kenosha, WI 53140, or call 262-653-2542. Its jobs include administering the property tax laws, collecting delinquent tax, and the yearly settlement with the municipalities, school districts, Gateway Technical College and the Wisconsin Department of Revenue.

Two counters take later installments and delinquent tax in person. One is the downtown office on 56th Street, open 8 am to 5 pm weekdays. The other is the Elected Officials Office at the Kenosha County Center in Bristol, at the crossing of Highways 45 and 50, open 8 am to 4:30 pm weekdays. Wis. Stat. 74.11(6) divides the money this way: payment on or before January 31 goes to the municipal treasurer, and everything else goes to the county treasurer unless the bill directs otherwise.

A Property Inquiry portal, linked from the county's Property & Taxes page, shows a parcel's bills, assessments, sales and building data along with current and historical county mill rates.

Due dates

Pay everything, or the first installment, on or before January 31. After that the route depends on where the parcel is.

Where the parcel isInstallmentsPay to
City of KenoshaFull payment, or three installments due Jan 31, Apr 30 and Jul 31City of Kenosha through July 31
Village of Pleasant PrairieFull payment, or three installments due Jan 31, Apr 30 and Jul 31Village of Pleasant Prairie through July 31
All other municipalitiesFull payment or first installment by Jan 31Local town or village treasurer for Jan 31; Kenosha County Treasurer for the second installment and anything delinquent

Mid-December is when bills go out, and 74.09(5) requires the mailing by the third Monday of December. No bill by about December 20? Phone your municipal treasurer, since 74.09(6) says a bill that never came is not an excuse for paying late.

January 31, 2027 is a Sunday. In that situation the five-working-day grace period stretches to the first Friday of February (74.11(7)(b) and 74.12(7)(b)), here February 5, 2027. Check the exact cutoff with your treasurer first.

Missing a payment

A missed payment makes the full unpaid balance delinquent and ends the installment option. Skip the first installment and the whole remaining tax is delinquent on February 1 (74.11(7) and 74.12(7)). Skip July 31 and the unpaid balance is delinquent on August 1, with interest and penalty counted back to February 1.

Under 74.47(1), interest is 1 percent a month, and any part of a month counts as a full month. A county may add a 0.5 percent monthly penalty by ordinance (74.47(2)). Kenosha County quotes the two together as 18 percent a year. Because state law fixes the amounts, the treasurer's office has no power to change them.

Delinquent tax from earlier years is always paid at the County Treasurer's Office, which offers a payment plan with these terms:

  • Each delinquent year gets 10 months, so a single year means 10 months and two years mean 20.
  • Three years of delinquency begin the tax deed foreclosure process, and the owner can lose the property.
  • You must also pay current-year installments on time while the plan runs.
  • A skipped plan payment, or current-year tax that turns delinquent, cancels the plan and the entire balance comes due. Two skipped plan payments cancel it too.

If you own in the City of Kenosha or Pleasant Prairie and are behind on this year's tax, call your local treasurer up to July 31 and the County Treasurer from then on.

How to pay

You have four ways to pay, with a few traps for mailed and online payments.

  • By mail: return the stub from the top of the bill with your payment. Add a self-addressed stamped envelope to get a receipt. Close to a deadline, hand the envelope to a post office clerk and request a hand postmark. A check sent through a bank's bill-pay service frequently carries no postmark, and the bank's confirmation does not prove you were on time.
  • In person: either county office takes cash, checks, money orders and cashier's checks, and credit cards as well.
  • Online: open the Property Inquiry portal and enter the 13-digit parcel identification number on your bill. Credit cards add a fee, and electronic check is available.
  • By phone: 1-888-891-6064, extension 2.

74.69(1) counts a payment as timely when the envelope is correctly addressed, prepaid, postmarked by the due date, and delivered within five working days after it. A mortgage escrow does not shift responsibility from you. Confirm the lender really paid, and be wary of telling the county to send every notice to the mortgage company.

Challenging your assessment

Because the municipality where the property sits sets the value, that is where an appeal begins. Every Board of Review meets once a year inside a 45-day window starting the fourth Monday of April, and not earlier than 7 days after the assessment roll closes for examination (70.47(1)). Notice has to be published at least 15 days ahead of the first session, or 30 days in a revaluation year (70.47(2)).

To be heard, tell the board clerk, in writing or aloud, at least 48 hours before the first session that you will object. Then hand in the written objection during the first two hours of that session (70.47(7)(a)). If you own land with improvements, the objection can address only their combined value. Still unhappy with the result? A court action for certiorari is next, and it has to begin within 90 days of receiving the board's notice (70.47(13)).

To get ready for next year, ask your municipal assessor when open book is held and which clerk takes Board of Review filings.

Credits and relief programs

The Wisconsin Lottery and Gaming Credit is for owners who lived in the home as their primary residence on January 1. A Lottery Credit search on the county's Property & Taxes page lets you verify you are getting it, and either the county treasurer or your municipal treasurer can mail an application. Once on a property, the credit stays until the owner or the Department of Revenue takes it off. Claims filed late, after the first installment date, require uploading a copy of your newest tax bill before October 1.

Owners with lower incomes can look into the Homestead Credit, claimed with state income taxes. Disabled service members and surviving spouses may qualify for another state property tax credit through the County service office. Interest cannot be forgiven by the treasurer for hardship.

Taxes when you sell

Most purchase contracts split the sale year's tax between seller and buyer. Without such a term, Wis. Stat. 74.15 has the seller reimburse the buyer one-twelfth of the preceding year's taxes for each month before the conveyance, counting the sale month if the deed date is after the 15th. Prepayment is possible too: from August 1 until the third Monday of December the municipal treasurer takes tax ahead of the levy (74.13).

For a delinquent parcel, the County Treasurer provides the payoff, with interest and penalty to the closing date. Request a written figure at 262-653-2542 that is good through your expected closing day. Special assessments and special charges are collected like the tax itself, and an unpaid special charge can make the entire parcel delinquent (74.11(10)(b)).

Selling to a cash buyer changes none of this. The tax payoff still comes from your proceeds, though with no lender the calendar is often shorter.

Kenosha County for homeowners

In the far southeast of Wisconsin on the western shore of Lake Michigan, Kenosha County has Racine County to the north and Walworth County to the west. Metra's Union Pacific North Line runs to Chicago. The population of 168,448 ranks eighth among Wisconsin counties. Median owner-occupied home value is $265,500, owners live in 66.7 percent of homes, median household income is $81,239 and median gross rent is $1,219. Besides the City of Kenosha, there are villages such as Pleasant Prairie, Bristol, Paddock Lake, Salem Lakes and Twin Lakes, and towns such as Brighton, Paris, Randall and Wheatland.

Frequently asked questions

When are Kenosha County property taxes due?

Pay the full amount or first installment by January 31. Later installments go to the County Treasurer, except in the City of Kenosha and Village of Pleasant Prairie, which take three installments (Jan 31, Apr 30, Jul 31) and keep current-year payments until July 31.

What interest does Kenosha County charge on late property tax?

1 percent a month under Wis. Stat. 74.47(1), plus a 0.5 percent monthly penalty, together listed by the county as 18 percent a year. It reaches back to February 1, and the treasurer cannot waive it.

Can I get a payment plan for delinquent Kenosha County taxes?

Yes, for prior-year taxes. The County Treasurer allows 10 months for each delinquent year, with current-year installments paid on time. Three years of delinquency begins tax deed foreclosure.

Where do I pay Kenosha County property tax online?

Go through the Property Inquiry portal linked on the county's Property & Taxes page, using the 13-digit parcel number on your bill. Cards carry a fee. City of Kenosha parcels pay the city, not the county, through July 31.

How do I appeal my Kenosha County assessment?

Call your municipal assessor, then use the municipal Board of Review. Tell the clerk 48 hours ahead of the first meeting and file in writing within its first two hours (Wis. Stat. 70.47(7)(a)). A court action by certiorari must start within 90 days of the board's notice.
